Brand: Trivora-NB Smartules
Molecule / composition: Glycopyrronium 12.5 µg + formoterol 6 µg +
  budesonide 800 µg — unit-dose nebulisation suspension, 2 mL ampoule
Therapeutic area: Respiratory — COPD
Indication: Maintenance therapy in moderate-to-severe COPD with ≥1
  exacerbation in the prior 12 months, across the hospital-to-home continuum

STATED POPULATION (the gate — be exact):
Indian adults ≥40 years, spirometry-confirmed moderate-to-severe COPD
(GOLD 2–3), with ≥1 documented exacerbation in the prior 12 months.
Named sub-cohort of strategic interest: women ≥40 with biomass-exposure-
related COPD.
Only age-agnostic evidence, or evidence in adults ≥40 with COPD, may carry
a claim.

Business objective (what must move, by when, by how much):
Move Trivora-NB from step-up therapy to first-line maintenance initiation.
Target: 20% quarterly Rx growth in metro and tier-1 across four quarters
post-campaign, with tier-2 entry from Q2. Hold volume share against
free-mix nebulisation.

Competitive set (what the narrative must displace):
- Free-mix nebulisation — separate budesonide, formoterol and
  glycopyrronium ampoules combined at the point of care
- Dual ICS/LABA nebulised maintenance
- ICS/LABA/LAMA triple therapy delivered by pMDI and DPI
- Generic budesonide respules

Evidence in hand — attached (see test-source-pack.md):
  [1] BREATH trial — randomised, open-label, interim analysis at discharge
  [2] Drug utilisation study — 2,477 patients, data on file
  [3] PROMs study — CSR NIS/2025/32, 2,366 patients
  [4] Hospital EMR exacerbation study — NIS/2026/12, 170 patients

Evolving / new evidence (in press, recent readouts, emerging RWD):
BREATH 6-month follow-up expected Q4. No data available yet.
Emerging interest in cardiovascular risk in the 30 days following an
exacerbation — signal only, no dedicated study in hand.

Guidelines in play:
GOLD 2026; Indian Chest Society / NCCP COPD guidance; ICMR.
No guideline text is attached.

In-house HCP insights (10-doctor dipstick survey — pulmonologists and
consultant physicians, metro and tier-1):
  1. "Triple is what I move to when dual stops working." Triple therapy is
     read as rescue or step-up, not as first-line maintenance.
  2. Success is judged by symptom relief at follow-up, not by how long the
     patient stays exacerbation-free.
  3. "I can titrate better when I mix it myself." Free-mixing is believed
     to give finer dose control, and to cost the patient less.
  4. Nebulisation is seen as a hospital modality. Low confidence that
     patients will continue it correctly at home.
  5. Women presenting with biomass-exposure COPD are frequently labelled
     chronic bronchitis or asthma and not spirometry-confirmed.
  6. In tier-2, the cost objection is raised before the efficacy objection.

Target specialties: Pulmonologists; consultant physicians / internal
  medicine; critical care intensivists. Tier-2 and tier-3 GPs secondary.
HCP tiers / status mix: KOL, senior consultant, early-career
Geography and city tiers: Pan-India. Metro and tier-1 lead; tier-2 from Q2.
  South and West skew.

Price and access context:
Approximately 2.2× the per-day cost of free-mix nebulisation. Largely
out-of-pocket. Reimbursement limited to insured inpatient admission.
Tier-2 and tier-3 patients on long-duration maintenance are highly
price-sensitive.

MLR constraints (claims that cannot be made, and why):
- No superiority claim against free-mix nebulisation. No head-to-head
  trial exists.
- BREATH is interim and open-label. It may not be presented as definitive.
- Data on file must be labelled as such.
- No comparative safety claims.
- No promotion outside the approved indication.
- Vancouver-numbered inline references throughout.
- No patient-directed claims in HCP assets.

Deliverable: HCP-facing scientific strategy deck
Hard slide maximum, references slide included: 12
```
